title: Activity Selection Problem
description: Learn how greedy scheduling selects the maximum number of non-overlapping activities through earliest-finish-time optimization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Activity Selection Problem is one of the most well-known applications of Greedy Algorithms.

The goal is to select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities.

Each activity has a start time and finish time, but only one activity can be performed at a time.

This problem demonstrates how local greedy decisions can produce globally optimal scheduling solutions.

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems involve scheduling limited resources. Classrooms, airport runways, meeting rooms, CPU processors, and manufacturing systems cannot handle multiple overlapping tasks simultaneously.

Efficient scheduling improves productivity, resource usage, and execution efficiency.

The Activity Selection Problem models this challenge computationally.
bullets: Introduces compatibility checking and interval scheduling.

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Suppose we are given the following activities:

A1 = (1, 4)
A2 = (3, 5)
A3 = (0, 6)
A4 = (5, 7)
A5 = (8, 9)

Each activity contains a start time and finish time.

The objective is to select the maximum number of compatible activities.

Two activities are compatible if their time intervals do not overlap.

sections.title: Understanding Overlapping Activities
sections.content:
Suppose we first select activity A1 = (1, 4).

Activity A2 = (3, 5) cannot be selected afterward because 3 is less than 4.

This means A2 begins before A1 finishes, creating a scheduling conflict.

The algorithm must therefore carefully choose compatible activities.

sections.title: Core Greedy Idea
sections.content:
The greedy strategy is simple: always select the activity that finishes earliest.

At first, this may seem unusual. Choosing the earliest finishing activity maximizes the remaining time available for future activities.

This increases the chance of selecting additional compatible activities later.

sections.title: Why Earliest Finishing Works
sections.content:
Suppose we select an activity that finishes very late, such as (1, 10). This blocks many future activities.

However, if we instead choose an activity such as (1, 3), more scheduling space remains afterward.

The greedy strategy succeeds because early finishing preserves maximum scheduling flexibility.

This is the key intuition behind the algorithm.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Example
sections.content:
Suppose activities are sorted by finish time:

A1 = (1, 4)
A2 = (3, 5)
A3 = (0, 6)
A4 = (5, 7)
A5 = (8, 9)

The algorithm first selects A1 because it finishes earliest.

A2 overlaps with A1 because 3 is less than 4, so A2 is skipped.

A3 also overlaps with A1, so it is skipped as well.

A4 becomes compatible because 5 is greater than or equal to 4, so A4 is selected.

Finally, A5 is compatible with A4 because 8 is greater than or equal to 7.

The final selected activities become A1, A4, and A5.

sections.title: Timeline Visualization
sections.content:
Visualizing activity intervals helps explain overlap detection and scheduling compatibility.

A1: |----|
A2: |----|
A3: |------|
A4: |---|
A5: |-|

Selected schedule:
A1 → A4 → A5

The visualization shows how compatible activities avoid overlap.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Activity Selection implementations usually sort activities by finish time before greedily selecting compatible intervals.

codeSnippets.title: Activity Selection implementation
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [
    (1, 4),
    (3, 5),
    (0, 6),
    (5, 7),
    (8, 9)
]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

selected = []
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        selected.append((start, finish))
        last_finish = finish

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Count compatible activities
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (4, 6), (6, 8)]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

count = 0
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        count += 1
        last_finish = finish

print(count)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Sorting activities by finish time requires O(n log n) complexity.

After sorting, the algorithm performs only one linear traversal to select compatible activities.

This creates overall O(n log n) complexity.

Space complexity is usually O(1) because only a few tracking variables are required.

chart.title: Activity Selection complexity
chart.description: Sorting dominates the runtime of Activity Selection, while compatibility checking only requires linear traversal afterward.

sections.title: Why This Problem Is Greedy
sections.content:
The Activity Selection Problem satisfies the Greedy Choice Property.

Choosing the earliest finishing activity never reduces future scheduling opportunities.

Instead, early finishing preserves the maximum remaining time for additional compatible activities.

This is why the greedy strategy works correctly for this problem.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The Activity Selection Problem appears in CPU scheduling, classroom scheduling, airline runway allocation, manufacturing systems, operating systems, conference management, and cloud infrastructure scheduling.

Many modern scheduling systems rely heavily on greedy optimization strategies.

subsections.title: Mistake: Selecting earliest starting activities
subsections.content: Starting earlier does not guarantee maximum scheduling flexibility. Earliest finishing activities preserve more future time.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring sorting
subsections.content: The greedy strategy depends on finish-time ordering.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect overlap checking
subsections.content: Activities are compatible only if current.start is greater than or equal to previous.finish.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The Activity Selection Problem maximizes compatible activities.
The greedy strategy selects the earliest finishing activity first.
Early finishing maximizes future scheduling flexibility.
Sorting by finish time is essential.
The algorithm achieves O(n log n) complexity.
